app.name: Physics Bench
app.description: A virtual physics laboratory: perform real practicals on a 3D bench, record your own readings, plot your graph and write your lab report.

stretched-wire.title: Resonant frequency of a stretched wire and its length
stretched-wire.aim: To investigate how the resonant frequency of a stretched wire depends on its vibrating length when the tension is kept constant, and to find the wire's mass per unit length.
theory: A wire stretched between two bridges vibrates in standing waves with nodes at the bridges. In its fundamental mode the vibrating length $l$ is half a wavelength, so $\lambda = 2l$.
Transverse waves travel along a wire of tension $T$ and mass per unit length $\mu$ at speed $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$. With $v = f\lambda$, the fundamental frequency is
At constant tension $f \propto 1/l$: a graph of $f$ against $1/l$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $k = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{T/\mu}$, so $\mu = \dfrac{T}{4k^{2}}$ with $T = Mg$.
When the wire's natural frequency matches the tuning fork's, it resonates: a small paper rider placed at the middle of the wire (an antinode of the fundamental) is thrown off.

apparatus.sonometer: Sonometer: a hollow wooden box with a wire fixed at one end, running over two bridges and a pulley.
apparatus.forks: Set of tuning forks, 256–512 Hz, each stamped with its frequency.
apparatus.pad: Rubber pad for striking the forks.
apparatus.rider: Paper rider: a small V of paper that sits on the wire.
apparatus.masses: Hanger and slotted masses to set the tension.
apparatus.rule: Metre rule fixed along the sonometer, read to the nearest millimetre.

safety: Keep your feet clear of the hanging load and add masses gently.
Strike forks only on the rubber pad, never on the bench or the sonometer.
steps: Hang a load on the wire and record its total mass M (hanger included).
Place the paper rider at the middle of the wire between the bridges.
Start with the movable bridge close to the fixed bridge (short length).
Strike the lowest-frequency fork on the rubber pad and press its stem on the sonometer box.
Slowly lengthen the wire until the rider is thrown off. Read the bridge position: this is l₁.
Start long and shorten the wire until the rider is thrown again: this is l₂.
Repeat for every fork, keeping the load the same.
Work out l = (l₁ + l₂)/2 and 1/l in m⁻¹, then plot f against 1/l.
tips: Read the rule square-on (Eye level view) to avoid parallax.
Near resonance, move the bridge in small steps and strike the fork again: the rider only jumps while the fork is loud.
If the rider is thrown at a length much longer than expected, the wire may be vibrating in two loops.
references: Young, H. D. & Freedman, R. A. University Physics, ch. 15: Mechanical waves (standing waves on a string).
Physics Bench virtual laboratory — sonometer practical.

why.voltmeter: Nothing electrical is measured: the frequency is stamped on each fork and the length is read on the rule.
why.stopwatch: No timing is needed — the fork's frequency is known.
why.horseshoe-magnet: A magnet drives the wire in the AC-sonometer practical. Here the fork drives it.

resonance-tube-two.title: Velocity of sound in air by resonance tube
resonance-tube-two.aim: To determine the velocity of sound in air from the first and second resonance positions of a tube closed at one end, and to find the end correction.

why.signal-generator: A tuning fork gives the known frequency here; the signal generator is for the narrow-neck resonator.
why.measuring-cylinder: You measure lengths of the air column, not volumes.

resonance-tube-forks.title: Velocity of sound in an air column closed at one end
resonance-tube-forks.aim: To determine the velocity of sound in air and the end correction of a closed tube using tuning forks of different frequencies.

why.signal-generator: A tuning fork gives the known frequency here; the signal generator is for the narrow-neck resonator.
why.measuring-cylinder: You measure lengths of the air column, not volumes.

helmholtz.title: Calibration of a narrow-neck (Helmholtz) resonator
helmholtz.aim: To calibrate a narrow-neck resonator by measuring its resonant frequency for different air volumes, and to use the calibration to find an unknown volume.

why.tuning-forks: Forks give a few fixed frequencies; you need to sweep the frequency continuously to find each resonance.
why.metre-rule: Volumes come from the measuring cylinder; no lengths are measured.
why.oscilloscope: Not needed: you judge the loudest sound by ear (or on the sound-level meter).

hints.speaker: Connect the generator's output to the loudspeaker: output to + and earth (⏚) to −.

faraday.title: Induced emf and the rate of change of magnetic flux
faraday.aim: To investigate how the emf induced in a search coil depends on the rate of change of the magnetic flux linking it (Faraday's law).

why.dc-ammeter: The solenoid current alternates; a DC ammeter would read about zero. Use the a.c. ammeter.
why.bar-magnet: Here the changing flux comes from the alternating current in the solenoid, not a moving magnet.
why.voltmeter: The oscilloscope measures the induced emf (and shows its waveform).

hints.primaryLoop: The generator, a.c. ammeter and solenoid make one loop: generator → ammeter → solenoid → back to the generator.
hints.ammeterSeries: An ammeter goes in series: the solenoid's current must flow through it.
hints.coilToScope: The search coil connects only to the oscilloscope: one end to the Y input, the other to earth (⏚).

slinky.title: Magnetic field inside a slinky stretched to various lengths
slinky.aim: To investigate how the magnetic field at the centre of a current-carrying slinky depends on its length, and to determine the permeability of free space.

why.voltmeter: You need the current, not the voltage: the field depends on I.
why.step-down-transformer: An alternating current would make the field alternate; the teslameter reads steady fields.
why.compass: A compass is used in a different method (deflection); here the Hall probe measures B directly.

hints.loop: Everything is in one series loop: supply + → rheostat → ammeter → slinky → supply −.
hints.ammeterSeries: An ammeter goes in series, with its + terminal towards the supply's + side.
hints.rheostatSeries: The rheostat goes in series so it can set the current.

current-balance.title: Force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
current-balance.aim: To demonstrate the force on a current-carrying wire across a magnetic field and to show that it is proportional to the current.

why.voltmeter: You need the current through the rod, not the voltage.
why.step-down-transformer: With alternating current the force would alternate too fast for the balance to show.
why.slotted-masses: The balance measures the force directly; no masses are hung.

hints.loop: Everything is in one series loop: supply + → rheostat → ammeter → copper rod → supply −.
hints.ammeterSeries: An ammeter goes in series, with its + terminal towards the supply's + side.
hints.rheostatSeries: The rheostat goes in series so it can set the current.

ac-sonometer.title: Frequency of alternating current using a sonometer
ac-sonometer.aim: To determine the frequency of an alternating current supply using a sonometer wire carrying the current in a magnetic field.

why.tuning-forks: The supply sets the frequency here — that is the unknown you are measuring.
why.dc-supply: A steady current gives a steady force: the wire would be pushed aside once, not made to vibrate.
why.voltmeter: You do not need the voltage: only the length and tension at resonance.

hints.loop: The transformer, the switch and the sonometer wire form a single loop: transformer → switch → one end of the wire, and the other end of the wire back to the transformer.

enoughRows.title: {n} readings — a good number
enoughRows.detail: Enough points to draw a reliable line and spot a reading that doesn't fit.

tooFewRows.title: Only {n} complete readings
tooFewRows.detail: Take at least {min}. With few points one bad reading can tilt your whole line, and you can't tell which one it is.

narrowRange.title: Your readings cover a narrow range
narrowRange.detail: Your largest x value is only {ratio}× your smallest. Spread your readings over as wide a range as the apparatus allows so the slope is well defined.

unparseable.title: “{value}” in column {symbol} isn't a number
unparseable.detail: Type only the number in the cell; the unit belongs in the column header.

inconsistentDecimals.title: Column {symbol} mixes precisions
inconsistentDecimals.detail: Values are written to {list} decimal places. Readings from one instrument should all be recorded to the same precision.

falsePrecision.title: Too many digits in {symbol}
falsePrecision.detail: Your instrument can only be read to {expected} decimal place(s) in {unit}. Extra digits claim a precision you didn't measure.

underRecorded.title: Digits dropped in {symbol}
underRecorded.detail: The instrument reads to {expected} decimal place(s) in {unit}. Record the last digit even when it is 0 (write 45.0, not 45).

unitSlip.title: {value} in column {symbol} looks like a different unit
unitSlip.detail: It is about {factor}× away from the rest of the column. Was it recorded in another unit?

derivedArithmetic.title: {count} value(s) of {symbol} don't follow from your readings
derivedArithmetic.detail: For example you wrote {typed}, but your readings give {expected} {unit}. Re-check the arithmetic and the unit conversion.

outlier.title: A point lies {sigma}σ from the line
outlier.detail: This reading doesn't fit the pattern of the others. Repeat it before you decide anything about it.

noTitle.title: Your graph needs a title
noTitle.detail: Name what is plotted against what, e.g. “Graph of f against 1/l”.

noAxisLabel.title: The {axis}-axis has no label
noAxisLabel.detail: Label every axis with the quantity and its unit.

axisNoUnit.title: The {axis}-axis label has no unit
axisNoUnit.detail: Write the unit with the quantity, e.g. “… / {unit}”.

awkwardScale.title: {perSquare} per square on the {axis}-axis is hard to plot with
awkwardScale.detail: Choose 1, 2 or 5 (×10ⁿ) units per square so every point falls where you can read it.

offPaper.title: Some points fall off the {axis}-axis
offPaper.detail: Extend the scale so every reading fits on the paper.

smallScale.title: Your plot only reaches {percent}% of the {axis}-axis
smallScale.detail: Choose a scale that makes the plot fill at least half the paper in each direction; a bigger graph gives a more precise slope.

noLine.title: Draw your best straight line
noLine.detail: Drag the two ends of the line so it follows the trend of your points.

lineTooSteep.title: Your line is about {percent}% steeper than your points suggest
lineTooSteep.detail: A best-fit line has roughly as many points above it as below, spread along its whole length.

lineTooShallow.title: Your line is about {percent}% shallower than your points suggest
lineTooShallow.detail: A best-fit line has roughly as many points above it as below, spread along its whole length.

missesCentroid.title: Your line misses the middle of your data
missesCentroid.detail: A best-fit line passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ) of your readings.

unbalanced.title: {above} points above your line, {below} below
unbalanced.detail: Try rotating the line slightly so the points are shared more evenly.

goodLine.title: Your best-fit line follows your data well
goodLine.detail: It passes through the middle of your points with them balanced on either side.

noTriangle.title: Mark a slope triangle on your line
noTriangle.detail: Pick two points on your line (not data points) far apart, and read Δy and Δx.

smallTriangle.title: Your slope triangle is small
smallTriangle.detail: Use a triangle covering at least half your line: reading errors matter less over a large Δx.

triangleOffLine.title: Your triangle's corners aren't on your line
triangleOffLine.detail: Take both points from your drawn line, not from the data.

noSlope.title: Calculate the slope of your line
noSlope.detail: Use your triangle: slope = Δy / Δx, with units.

unreadable.title: “{value}” isn't a number
unreadable.detail: Type the {what} as a number; units go beside it.

slopeOk.title: Your slope matches your graph
slopeOk.detail: Good — the value follows from your own triangle.

slopeInverted.title: Your slope is upside down
slopeInverted.detail: You worked out Δx / Δy. The slope is Δy / Δx: the change up divided by the change across.

slopeSign.title: Your slope has the wrong sign
slopeSign.detail: Check which way your line goes: rising lines have a positive slope.

slopeWrong.title: Your slope ({typed}) doesn't match your triangle
slopeWrong.detail: Your triangle gives about {expected}. Re-read Δy and Δx from the graph, in the units on your axes.

interceptFalseOrigin.title: Your intercept ({typed}) can't be read from this graph
interceptFalseOrigin.detail: Your x-axis doesn't start at zero, so the line crosses x = 0 off the paper. Calculate it: c = y − m·x using a point on your line (about {expected}).

interceptWrong.title: Your intercept ({typed}) doesn't match your line
interceptWrong.detail: Your line crosses x = 0 at about {expected}.

noPrecautions.title: List your precautions
noPrecautions.detail: What did you do to make your readings reliable? Each precaution should be something you actually did.

fewPrecautions.title: Only {n} precaution(s)
fewPrecautions.detail: Most practicals have three or more worth stating.

precautionsTense.title: Write precautions as things you did
precautionsTense.detail: “The rider was placed at the middle of the wire”, not “the rider should be placed…”.

noSources.title: Name your sources of error
noSources.detail: Which effects could have made your result differ from the true value, and in which direction?

vagueSources.title: “Human error” isn't a source of error
vagueSources.detail: Name the actual effect: parallax when reading the rule, judging the exact point of resonance, fork frequency tolerance…

noConclusion.title: Write a conclusion
noConclusion.detail: Answer the aim in one or two sentences, with your result and its unit.

conclusionNoValue.title: State your result in the conclusion
conclusionNoValue.detail: Include the value you obtained, with its unit.

secondHarmonic.title: This length is about twice what the other forks suggest
secondHarmonic.detail: The wire may have been vibrating in its second harmonic (two loops). Keep the rider at the middle of the wire and start from a short length.

halfLength.title: This length is about half what the other forks suggest
halfLength.detail: Check that you read the distance between the two bridges, not from one bridge to the rider.

inverseInCm.title: 1/l worked out with l in centimetres
inverseInCm.detail: Convert l to metres first: l = 44.6 cm = 0.446 m, so 1/l = 2.24 m⁻¹ (not 0.0224).

approachesDisagree.title: Your two approaches to resonance disagree
approachesDisagree.detail: l₁ and l₂ for the same fork differ by more than 8 mm. Repeat, moving the bridge slowly near resonance.

approachesIdentical.title: l₁ and l₂ are identical in every row
approachesIdentical.detail: Approaching resonance from a short length and from a long length usually gives slightly different readings. Did you take both?

struckOnBench.title: Fork struck on the bench {n} time(s)
struckOnBench.detail: Striking a fork on a hard surface can damage it and produces overtones. Strike it on the rubber pad.

scaleNotLength.title: {n} reading(s) look like the scale position, not the length
scaleNotLength.detail: The vibrating length is the distance between the bridges: the scale reading at the movable bridge minus the fixed bridge's position ({fixed} cm).

transposed.title: {n} reading(s) have two digits swapped
transposed.detail: What you wrote has the same digits as the rule showed, in a different order. Read the rule again and copy carefully.

wrongPicks.title: {n} item(s) picked that this practical does not use
wrongPicks.detail: Before a practical, read the apparatus list against the method and the theory: each item must have a job in the experiment.

circuitAttempts.title: The circuit took {n} tries to get right
circuitAttempts.detail: Draw the circuit diagram first, then wire it one loop at a time: ammeters in series with what they measure, meters to the instrument they serve.

clean.title: Apparatus chosen and set up correctly first time
clean.detail: Good preparation makes the measurements go smoothly.

start.title: How do you want to work?
start.performBody: Set up the sonometer, strike the forks and read the rule yourself. Each session has its own wire and forks.
start.bringBody: Type in the readings you took in a real lab and get the same analysis and feedback.
start.notReady: This practical's bench is being built. You can read the brief now; recording data opens when it is ready.

panel.noActions: Nothing done on the bench yet.
panel.liveEmpty: Nothing to flag on this stage yet.

graph.title: Graph
graph.label: Label
graph.hint: Drag the ends of your line until it fits your points. Then mark a slope triangle on it.

calculate.title: Calculations
calculate.resultFrom: Using your slope and your recorded load
calculate.noLine: Draw your best-fit line on the graph first.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.discussionHint: Analyse and interpret your graph. Is f proportional to 1/l? What does the intercept tell you? Explain your result using the theory.
discussion.precautionsHint: What did you do to make your readings reliable? One per line.
discussion.sourcesHint: Which effects could make your result differ from the true value? One per line.
discussion.conclusionHint: Answer the aim with your result and its unit.

feedback.title: Feedback
feedback.allClear: Nothing to fix. Compare is now open.

compare.title: Compare
compare.fair: Outside the {n}% a careful run achieves. Look at your feedback for where it crept in.
compare.noAccepted: No accepted value: in bring-your-data mode the wire's true μ isn't known. Compare with the value stated for your wire, or with classmates.
compare.overlay: Dashed: a careful run in the same apparatus
compare.hidden: Hidden apparatus values for this session
compare.fork: Fork stamped {nominal} Hz really vibrated at {actual} Hz

report.title: Lab report
report.intro: Your report follows the 15-section format. Facts come from your session; the writing is yours.
report.name: Your name

setup.intro: Collect what this practical needs from the shelf. Some things on the shelf belong to other practicals. Then, if there is a circuit, wire it yourself.
setup.wiringHint: Click a terminal, then another terminal, to connect them with a lead. Click a lead to remove it. Then check your circuit.
setup.wrong: Not quite — some connections are wrong.
setup.ready: Your apparatus is set up. Time to measure.

trainer.title: Practise significant figures
trainer.count: How many significant figures are in {number}?
trainer.record: A {instrument} reads exactly {truth} {unit}. Write the reading as you would record it (number only, in {unit}).

why.count: Non-zero digits count (rule 1); zeros between them count (rule 2); trailing zeros after the decimal point count (rule 3); leading zeros never count. In standard form, only the digits before × 10ⁿ count.
why.round: Rounded, with every significant zero kept.
why.roundValue: Look at the first digit you drop: 5 or more rounds the last kept digit up.
why.roundZeros: The value is right but the number of figures is not: keep trailing zeros that are significant (0.500, not 0.5).
why.recordValue: That is not what the instrument shows.
why.recordDropped: A reading exactly on a mark still has its last digit: write the 0 (e.g. 45.0 cm on a mm-scale rule). Dropping it throws away precision you measured.
why.recordFalse: That claims more precision than the instrument can give: stop at the digit the scale lets you read.

report.title: Report format
report.intro: The default is the 15-section format. Rename, reorder or leave out sections to match your school's format; reports and Word exports follow it.
